title: Write clearly without losing your voice
description: A practical way to make a rough first draft easier to read while keeping the words that make it yours.
content: The best first draft is usually the one that arrives before you can second-guess it. Let it be rough. Clarity comes in the next pass.
Read your draft once for the point. Can someone tell what you need, think, or want them to do? Then read it for the human parts: the detail, rhythm, and point of view that make it sound like you.
Cut what repeats. Name the next step. Keep the sentence that only you could have written. A clearer message should still feel familiar when it reaches the person reading it.

title: A better way to start an email
description: Start with context and make the purpose easy to find, so your reader knows where the message is going.
content: A strong email opening does not need to be clever. It needs to give the reader enough context to understand why this message is in their inbox.
Use the first two sentences to connect the message to a conversation, project, or decision. Then make your request or update clear.
This simple sequence helps people respond with less effort and keeps the conversation moving.

title: Make LinkedIn posts sound like you
description: A simple editing pass that brings a professional post closer to the way you naturally speak.
content: Write the first version as if you were telling one thoughtful person what happened and why it mattered. That gives you a useful starting point before you shape it for a wider audience.
Keep the specific moment, lesson, or question. Remove phrases you would never say out loud. Read it once at a normal speaking pace.
Professional writing can still be personal. The clearest posts give readers something real to hold on to.
